# 028 · A retry helper that sleeps out the Retry-After delay gives a pure module a thread call

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: 2 capability changes** | performance, determinism | high | feature, behaviour change not intended | [`RetryPolicy#retryAfterWaiting`](../../../examples/demo/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/retry/RetryPolicy.java) | [B10: Capability contracts](../../../lib/README.md) |

> The kernels in this module decide and never wait: the retry policy returns whether to retry, and the client's scheduler does the waiting. A developer adds a convenience that waits out the server's `Retry-After` delay with `Thread.sleep` and then decides, so that a client filter can retry inline. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `threads`, and the build fails: the module can now block the thread it is called on.

## The change

Add `retryAfterWaiting`, which sleeps for the delay the server asked for and then returns `shouldRetry`. The existing method is untouched, the new one is a few lines, and it saves every caller from wiring a scheduler. No test is added, because the method is a sleep followed by a call that is already tested.

**Before** ([`RetryPolicy.java`](../../../examples/demo/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/retry/RetryPolicy.java), line 25):

```java
        }
        return status == 408 || (status >= 500 && status <= 599 && status != 501);
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
        }
        return status == 408 || (status >= 500 && status <= 599 && status != 501);
    }

    /**
     * {@link #shouldRetry}, after waiting out the delay the server asked for ({@code Retry-After}), so that a client
     * filter can retry inline without a scheduler of its own.
     */
    public static boolean retryAfterWaiting(int status, boolean idempotent, int attempt, int maxAttempts, long delayMillis) {
        try {
            Thread.sleep(delayMillis);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            return false;
        }
        return shouldRetry(status, idempotent, attempt, maxAttempts);
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

The module's bytecode now reaches 2 capabilities differently from its contract:

| Capability | The contract lists | The bytecode now has |
|---|---|---|
| `threads` | *(nothing)* | `net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry.RetryPolicy.retryAfterWaiting calls java.lang.Thread.interrupt` |
| `threads` | *(nothing)* | `net.terminalvalue.crosscut.retry.RetryPolicy.retryAfterWaiting calls java.lang.Thread.sleep` |

Every call from the module's compiled code to a JDK entry point of a capability is listed, with the method that makes it, so the finding points at the exact call site.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

A call that sleeps is a call that holds whatever thread it is on. In a servlet container that is one of a few hundred request threads, held for the length of a dependency's `Retry-After`, which under load is exactly when the dependency asks for long waits; the pool drains and the service stops answering requests that have nothing to do with that dependency. On a WebFlux event loop it is worse: one sleeping call stalls every request on that loop, and Reactor's `BlockHound` would have failed the call outright. Under virtual threads a `Thread.sleep` is cheap, which is why the change looks harmless on a laptop in 2026, and why it reaches production. The policy module was pure precisely so that it could be used from any of these without knowing which.

## Why the verdict is right

The capability contract of the module is derived from its compiled classes: every call from the module's bytecode to a JDK entry point of a capability (the clock, randomness, threads, the network, reflection, ...), grouped by capability. The committed contract says `threads: none`, which is the module's promise never to block, spawn or sleep. The patched bytecode calls `Thread.sleep` and `Thread.interrupt` from `RetryPolicy.retryAfterWaiting`, and the contract check lists both call sites. This is a closed-world check over every instruction, not a lint: bytecode that never names an entry point of a capability cannot exercise it. Deriving it takes milliseconds and needs no JVM.

## What to do

Return the delay instead of waiting it out: `retryDelayMillis(...)` is as pure as `shouldRetry`, and the caller hands it to its own scheduler, `Mono.delay` on WebFlux, a `ScheduledExecutorService` or a virtual thread elsewhere. If a module really must gain a capability, `jvmcontract update` regenerates the contract and the diff names the new power and the call site, for a reviewer to approve.

## Evidence

The proof trusted these JDK APIs to be pure: `java.lang.Enum.ordinal`, `java.lang.MatchException.<init>`, `java.lang.Record.<init>`, `java.lang.runtime.SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch`, `java.util.List.copyOf`, `java.util.List.of`, `java.util.Objects.requireNonNull`.

**Provenance:** Constructed from the blocking-call-in-a-library mistake that Reactor's BlockHound exists to catch, placed in the one module of a service that is meant to be callable from anywhere.

- [Reactor, BlockHound: detecting blocking calls from non-blocking threads](https://github.com/reactor/BlockHound)
- [RFC 9110, section 10.2.3: the Retry-After header](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-10.2.3)
